summary: This informational memo from Cisco gives an overview of tag switching, a way of forwarding packets by looking up a short label instead of the full destination address. It describes the two main parts, forwarding and control. It is a vendor description, not a standard.

eli5.summary: Instead of reading the whole address on each package, the sorting room just reads a small colored sticker.

subtitle: A forwarding architecture that replaces IP lookups with label swapping for higher performance

tldr.problem: Internet routers were struggling with forwarding performance and the scaling of routing tables as the internet grew. More sophisticated routing functions like multicast and traffic engineering were hard to support.
tldr.mechanism: Tag switching separates routing (control) from forwarding (data). Instead of examining the full destination IP address on every hop, packets carry a short label (tag) that is swapped at each switch, using simple table lookups rather than complex address matching.
tldr.outcome: Tag switching was a Cisco vendor proposal that demonstrated the label-swapping concept but was not adopted as an IETF standard. The concepts influenced the later development of MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching), which became the standardized version.

today: RFC 2105 was Cisco's vendor-specific proposal and never became an IETF standard. However, the concepts proved influential. The later IETF standardization effort resulted in MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching, RFC 3031), which generalized and standardized the label-swapping architecture. MPLS became widely deployed in ISP networks and remains important for traffic engineering and fast reroute today.

sections.title: The Problem and Tag Switching Solution
sections.content:
Tag switching addresses challenges facing Internet Service Providers in the mid-1990s: growing demand for bandwidth, the need for higher forwarding performance (more packets per second), and limitations of traditional IP routing for advanced functions like multicast and traffic engineering.

Tag switching blends the flexibility of network-layer routing with the simplicity of label swapping. The core insight is that instead of examining the full destination address on every router hop, packets carry a short label (tag) that is swapped at each hop. This simpler forwarding paradigm enables higher performance and flexible routing functionality while maintaining the scalability of IP routing.

The architecture consists of two main components: a forwarding component that performs simple label swapping, and a control component that manages label bindings using existing routing protocols like OSPF and BGP.
sections.eli5: Regular IP routing reads the whole destination address at each router and figures out where the packet goes. Tag switching puts a quick label on the packet instead, and each router just swaps the label for the next one, which is much faster.

sections.title: Forwarding with Label Swapping
sections.content:
The forwarding component uses exact match on a fixed-length tag instead of the longest-match lookups required for IP addresses. When a tag switch receives a tagged packet, it looks up the tag in its Tag Information Base (TIB). Each TIB entry maps an incoming tag to one or more outgoing tags, outgoing interfaces, and link-level information.

The switch replaces the packet's tag with an outgoing tag, updates the link-level information (such as MAC addresses), and forwards the packet. This is simpler than IP forwarding and can be implemented directly in hardware, enabling much higher packets-per-second throughput.

Tags can be carried in multiple ways: as a small shim header between Layer 2 and Network Layer headers, as part of the Layer 2 header (like in ATM), or in the Network Layer header itself (like IPv6's Flow Label field). This flexibility allows tag switching to work over virtually any media type.
sections.eli5: The switch uses the tag as a quick index into a table that says what label to replace it with and which link to send it on. This is faster than looking at the destination IP address.

sections.title: Control Component and Tag Bindings
sections.content:
The control component creates tag bindings that associate tags with routing information. Tags can be bound at different granularities: to a group of destination prefixes, to a multicast tree, to an individual flow, or to an explicit route.

For destination-based routing, tag switches participate in routing protocols (OSPF, BGP) and build their Forwarding Information Base (FIB) just like regular routers. Tags are then allocated and bound to FIB entries using one of three methods: downstream allocation (tags allocated at the downstream end of a link), downstream on demand (tags allocated only when requested), or upstream allocation (tags allocated at the upstream end).

Tag bindings can be distributed by piggybacking on existing routing protocols or using a separate Tag Distribution Protocol (TDP). This decouples the control component from the forwarding component, allowing new routing functions to be added without changing the forwarding hardware.
sections.eli5: The control plane decides which tags go with which destinations and tells the switches how to swap them. This can be done by the routing protocols or a separate protocol.

sections.title: Advanced Routing Functions
sections.content:
Multicast support: Tag switches can bind tags to multicast trees. When forwarding a multicast packet, the switch uses tag swapping to forward to multiple outgoing interfaces, each with a potentially different outgoing tag. This allows the same simple forwarding algorithm to work for both unicast and multicast.

Hierarchical routing: By allowing a packet to carry a tag stack (multiple tags organized in a stack), tag switching can decouple interior routing from exterior routing. A packet carries two tags: the top tag routes to the egress border switch, while the second tag ensures correct forwarding within the destination domain. The stack is popped when appropriate.

Explicit routes and traffic engineering: Tag bindings can be manually configured to force packets along specific paths different from the destination-based routing paths. This allows ISPs to balance traffic across multiple links, avoiding congestion on heavily used links.
sections.eli5: The same label-swapping trick works for multicast, for routing between network domains, and for making packets follow specific paths you choose rather than just the shortest path.

sections.title: Integration with ATM and Deployment
sections.content:
Since ATM switches also use label swapping (swapping Virtual Circuit Identifiers), tag switching concepts can be directly applied to ATM. The tag information would be carried in the VCI field, with the VPI field available for a second level of tagging. This would allow ATM switches to participate in tag switching without needing separate ATM addressing and signaling schemes.

Tag switching can be deployed incrementally. Once a pair of adjacent routers is upgraded to support tag switching, they can exchange tags and use label swapping between themselves, while still interoperating with non-tag-switching routers. As more routers are upgraded, the benefits increase. Tag switches appear as regular routers to non-tag-switching devices since they use the same routing protocols.

Quality of service is also improved: once a packet is classified and assigned a tag, downstream switches can look up the tag to determine scheduling and queue behavior without re-classifying the packet based on headers.
sections.eli5: Tag switching works with ATM switches and can be rolled out gradually since the switches still talk to regular routers using normal routing protocols.
